'''''Dasylirion''''' is a genus of succulent, rosette-forming plants in the [[Asparagaceae]] family, where it is included in the subfamily [[Convallarioideae]]. Most species are native to mountainous arid regions of [[Mexico]], with some species also native to the [[Southwestern United States]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Dasylirion Zucc. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:24178-1#children |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Dasylirion in Flora of North America @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=109344 |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=www.efloras.org}}</ref> The common name '''sotol''' is used in English and Spanish to describe various ''Dasylirion'' species, as well as giving its name to [[sotol|a distilled spirit]] made from some species of the genus.<ref name=":2" /><ref name="RHSLG">{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for Gardeners |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |year=2012 |isbn=978-1845337315 |location=United Kingdom}}</ref>

The genus name ''Dasylirion'' is a compound word coming from the [[Greek language|Greek]] δασύς (''dasy''), meaning "dense, thick" or "shaggy" and λείριον (''lirion''), meaning "lily".<ref name=":2" /><ref name="RHSLG" />

As of November 2024, the genus ''Dasylirion'' includes 23 accepted species.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=WFO Plant List {{!}} World Flora Online |url=https://wfoplantlist.org/taxon/wfo-4000010824-2024-06?page=1 |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=wfoplantlist.org}}</ref>

== Description ==
Dasylirion are [[perennial]] and often long lived plants. With age, most form erect or reclining trunks that vary in height, depending on the species. The leaves blades are long-linear, evergreen and numerous, and are arranged into rosettes, living for several years and remaining persistent even after dying leading to the formation of a skirt around the plant. Some species have sharp and/or curved prickles along the leaf margins.<ref name=":2" />

Similar to ''[[Agave]]'', a genus in the same family and found in the same regions as ''Dasylirion'', the inflorescences consist of a tall stem or "mast" ("''[[Maguey flower|quiote]]''" in Mexico), which can grow several times the height of the plant, that grows apically from the center of the rosette. The flowers themselves are small and arranged in panicles at the end of the long, woody stem. Unlike most species of ''Agave'' that are [[monocarpic]], ''Dasylirion'' are [[polycarpic]] plants, meaning they do not die after flowering and may go on to flower many more times.<ref name=":2" />

''Dasylirion'' are [[dioecious]], with the male and female flowers on separate plants.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hernández-Quintero |first1=J.D. |last2=Reyes-Valdés |first2=M.H. |last3=Mendoza-Rodríguez |first3=D.V. |last4=Gómez-Martínez |first4=M. |last5=Rodríguez-Herrera |first5=R. |year=2015 |title=Study of the mitotic and meiotic chromosomes of sotol (''Dasylirion cedrosanum'' Trel.) |journal=Phyton |volume=84 |pages=107–112 |doi=10.32604/phyton.2015.84.107 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Native distribution ==
All 23 accepted species of ''Dasylirion'' are native to Mexico,<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Ruiz-Flores |first=Sara Isabel |last2=Castro-Castro |first2=Arturo |date=2024-10-11 |title=Distribución, riqueza, endemismo y conservación del género Dasylirion (Asparagaceae, Convallarioideae) |url=https://abm.ojs.inecol.mx/index.php/abm/article/view/2367 |journal=Acta Botanica Mexicana |language=es |issue=131 |doi=10.21829/abm131.2024.2367 |issn=2448-7589|doi-access=free }}</ref> with the genus covering much of the country from the border with the Southwestern United States to the border of [[Oaxaca]] in the south. Across Mexico, Dasylirion species are native to 20 states, with the greatest numbers found in [[San Luis Potosí]], followed by [[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]], [[Coahuila]] and [[Zacatecas]]. The typical habitat for most species are areas of transition between [[Xerophile|xerophilous]] shrublands and coniferous and ''Quercus'' (or [[oak]]) forests, such as the [[Sierra Madre Oriental pine–oak forests|Sierra Madre Oriental pine-oak forests]]. The greatest diversity in the genus is concentrated in the [[Sierra Madre Oriental]] where two regions of species richness are found (in common with both being centers of endemism), the first in the Gran Sierra Plegada, and the second in the arid zone between the states of [[Querétaro]] and [[Hidalgo (state)|Hidalgo]].<ref name=":4" />

Three species also considered native to the Southwestern United States: ''[[Dasylirion wheeleri]]'', commonly known as desert spoon in the USA, is native to [[Arizona]], [[New Mexico]], and [[Texas]], as well as Chihuahua and [[Sonora]] in Mexico;<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dasylirion wheeleri in Flora of North America @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242101561 |access-date=2024-11-27 |website=www.efloras.org}}</ref> ''[[Dasylirion texanum]]'', native to Texas as well as Coahuila, Mexico;<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dasylirion texanum in Flora of North America @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242101560 |access-date=2024-11-27 |website=www.efloras.org}}</ref> and ''[[Dasylirion leiophyllum]],'' native to New Mexico, Texas, as well as Chihuahua, and Coahuila in Mexico.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dasylirion leiophyllum in Flora of North America @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242101559 |access-date=2024-11-27 |website=www.efloras.org}}</ref>

== Human use ==
Dasylirion was once a major food source in the drier regions of the [[Southwestern United States|Southwest USA]] and Mexico.<ref name=":2" /> [[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]] would bake or roast the crown of the plant in rock-lined pits before drying and pounding to form a flour that was then made into cakes.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last=Facciola |first=Stephen |title=Cornucopia: a source book of edible plants |date=1990 |publisher=Kampong Publications |isbn=978-0-9628087-0-8 |location=Vista, CA}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Moerman |first=Daniel E. |title=Native American ethnobotany |date=1998 |publisher=Timber press |isbn=978-0-88192-453-4 |location=Portland (Or.)}}</ref> The flowering stems can also be roasted, boiled or eaten raw.<ref name=":5" />

The leaves were and are sometimes still used in thatching, basket making, and weaving into hats or mats.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":6" />

=== Sotol ===
[[File:Piñas de Sotol.jpg|300px|thumb|right|Sotol hearts being ready to roast.]]
[[Sotol]] is a [[Distilled beverage|distilled spirit]] produced from various species of ''Dasylirion''. The most common species used to produce sotol are ''[[Dasylirion wheeleri]]'', ''[[Dasylirion durangense]],'' ''[[Dasylirion cedrosanum]]'', and ''[[Dasylirion leiophyllum]],'' and less commonly with ''[[Dasylirion texanum]]'' and ''[[Dasylirion lucidum]]''.

Sotol has long been the most popular distilled spirit in the Mexican states of [[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]], [[Coahuila]], and [[Durango]], but sotol was technically illegal in Mexico until 1994. After legalization, it was granted a [[Denominación de origen|denomination of origin]] (DO) in 2002.<ref name=":0" /> According to the DO authorized by the [[Mexican Institute of Industrial Property]], Sotol can only be produced in Chihuahua, Coahuila, and Durango.

The indigenous peoples of the [[Chihuahuan Desert|Chihuahuan desert]], such as the [[Jumanos Pueblos|Jumano Pueblos]] and the [[Lipan Apache people|Lipan Apache]], have made this traditional drink for centuries.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" /> Other indigenous peoples of [[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]], such as the [[Rarámuri]], fermented sotol juice into a beer-like alcoholic beverage as early as 800 years ago.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |title=El boom del sotol, el licor que estuvo perseguido en México (y la polémica con los productores de Texas por quién puede elaborarlo) |url=https://www.bbc.com/mundo/noticias-america-latina-62101729 |access-date=2024-01-25 |work=BBC News Mundo |language=es}}</ref> After baking, the crown of the plant is peeled, crushed and mixed with water before being fermented.<ref name=":6" />

[[Distillation]] technology was introduced in the 16th century by early [[Filipino immigration to Mexico|Filipino immigrants]] who arrived via the [[Manila galleons]] to the coastal regions of western [[Mexico]]. Distinctive Filipino-type [[Still|stills]] were initially used by Filipino coconut farmers in distilling [[tubâ]] into "[[Lambanog|''vino de coco'']]" (coconut sap liquor). This technology and the knowledge of liquor production were acquired by the indigenous peoples who worked in the coconut plantations. They were then used to distil native drinks, resulting in sotol and the similarly produced [[mezcal]].<ref name="Bruman">{{cite journal |last1=Bruman |first1=Henry J. |date=July 1944 |title=The Asiatic Origin of the Huichol Still |journal=Geographical Review |volume=34 |issue=3 |pages=418 |doi=10.2307/209973}}</ref>
